title: Finite extensions and incomparable degrees

based_on.title: Computability theory
based_on.pages: Version 2024-02-25; §18.1, printed/PDF pp.74–75, Theorems18.1–18.2; finite-extension indices, opposite-bit choice and length growth made explicit

summary: Construct two membership problems that cannot decide one another, even though the halting oracle decides both.
abstract: The halting problem and its successive jumps form a rising chain of computational power, but such chains do not describe the whole order of Turing degrees. There are two membership problems neither of which can decide the other. We construct them by extending finite lists of membership answers. Each extension defeats one proposed oracle program, either by committing the opposite answer after a finite successful computation or by ensuring that the computation can never finish. Earlier commitments remain intact, so alternating between the two directions defeats every proposed reduction. A halting oracle can make the choices in this construction, placing both resulting degrees strictly between the computable degree and the halting degree. This does not yet give enumerable sets of intermediate degree: the construction uses the halting oracle to decide when no suitable finite extension exists.
